Don’t Just Tell Married Daughters to “Adjust” When They Complain of Cruelty: Allahabad High Court

The Allahabad High Court has cautioned families against routinely advising married daughters to “adjust”, “compromise” or “save the marriage” when they repeatedly complain of dowry harassment or cruelty.

The observations came while the Court upheld the conviction of a husband and four members of his family in a dowry-death case involving a 25-year-old woman and her 15-month-old daughter.

The Court observed that treating repeated complaints of harassment as ordinary matrimonial discord can unintentionally embolden perpetrators and expose a woman to continuing violence. A married daughter’s safety, dignity and well-being must be the family’s paramount concern, and repeated complaints should be taken seriously.

On the facts, the Court found that the prosecution had established the ingredients of dowry death, including cruelty linked to dowry demands soon before the woman’s unnatural death within seven years of marriage.

While affirming the convictions under Sections 304B and 498A IPC and the Dowry Prohibition Act, the High Court reduced the life sentences to the period already undergone, noting that the trial court had not given reasons for imposing the maximum punishment.
comment: A key practical issue is early intervention. Families and communities often become the first gatekeepers of justice; dismissing initial complaints can delay evidence, support systems, and timely legal protection.
